## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kākavatījātaka* (Ja 327) is a canonical Pali Jātaka tale, also known under the title *Kākāti Jātaka* [Harris 2005]. According to its traditional frame narrative (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha recounted the tale while residing at Jetavana to admonish a bhikkhu who was dissatisfied with his monastic life due to sensual passion; the Master remarked that women cannot be guarded, recounting how sages of the past placed a woman in a palace in the middle of the ocean beside Lake Simbali yet still failed to preserve her chastity. The core narrative concerns the abduction and seduction of a king's principal queen by a supernatural being, featuring the figure of Naṭakuvera [Harris 2005; Fausböll 1883]. Modern scholarship notes that the narrative shares its central theme with the *Sussondī Jātaka* (Ja 360) and served as inspiration for literary works in Southeast Asia, including court literature under King Ang Duang of Cambodia [Harris 2005].
